title: Effacement
hookLine: "others will be cruel; we will not be cruel here": forty-four resolves (MN 8)

cards: In almost any group there comes a moment when someone says: everyone does it. Everyone pads the expense report a little. Everyone talks about the boss when she's out of the room.
Everyone's a bit cruel online. It's hard to argue with, mostly because it's often a little true. A discourse in the Middle-Length Sayings has an answer to it, set out forty-four times.

teach.b: MN 8, the Sallekha. A monk named Mahacunda asks how to let go of the many views people hold about the self and the world. The Buddha's answer starts somewhere unexpected.
A monk might reach the jhanas, the deep meditative states, and think he's effacing. He isn't, the Buddha says; those are pleasant abidings, peaceful abidings, here and now.
Sallekha comes from a verb meaning to scrape away, to pare down: the slow whittling of what doesn't belong. Then the refrain.
Others will be cruel; we will not be cruel here: that is how you should efface. Others will kill living beings; we won't. Others will take what isn't given; we won't.
Others will speak falsely, maliciously, harshly, idly; we won't. Others will be envious, stingy, deceitful, arrogant, hard to correct; we won't.
Others will cling to their own views and let go only with difficulty; we won't. Forty-four in all. Two things stand out.
The refrain never adds: and they're terrible. It draws a line around your own conduct. And it doesn't wait for everyone else to agree first.
The Buddha gives a picture: as there might be an uneven road, and an even road to go around it, so not being cruel is the even road around cruelty.
The sutta ends with a line he repeats to many students: here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate. Don't delay, or you'll regret it later.

how: Theravada teachers often use the Sallekha Sutta's refrain as a model for personal resolves, and monastic training emphasizes keeping one's own conduct whatever others around one do.

o: the calm of deep meditation, the jhanas
a vow of silence kept during a retreat
effacement: paring away what doesn't belong

p: asks how to let go of views

s: MN 8 says the jhanas are the real effacement
they're pleasant, peaceful abidings; effacement is the refrain of resolves.
from cruelty and killing to clinging to one's own views.
the refrain condemns the others as wicked
it only draws a line around 'we, here'.

games.q: everyone at work pads their expense reports a little. in the spirit of MN 8, what's the line?
o: everyone does it, so it's fine
games.why: the refrain doesn't judge the others or wait for them. it simply says: here, we won't. that's effacement.

practice: Let the refrain run quietly, one line per breath: others may be harsh, I won't be harsh here; others may gossip, I won't gossip here; others may cling to their views, I won't cling here.
Then drop the words, and keep the one resolve that fits your week, like a smooth stone in your pocket.

wordCard.voice: Sallekha. Effacement: paring away what's unhelpful, line by line, whatever others are doing.

orig.note: Pali sallekha: effacement, paring down; from a verb meaning to scrape or pare.

carryVoice: Your line: others may, we won't. No waiting for everyone else to agree. See you tomorrow.
